comments.author: dang
comments.text: Related: OpenAI begins rolling out GPT-6 Astra - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49554273 How about we stick to that one for talking about the rollout, and this one for talking about the model?

comments.author: intenex
comments.text: The ARC-AGI-3 scorecard is extremely misleading given that it clearly states itself that "with [the responses API] harness, we estimate Sol would score in the ballpark of ~30%." but it shows a score of 7.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol presumably since if they updated the percentage for GPT-5.6 Sol to the score it would receive with the responses API harness they used for GPT-6 Astra they'd have to do the same for the percentage they show for Opus 5 which would similarly be much higher. Regardless, the result is still valid as the original benchmark harness is definitely unreasonably handicapped, and if a harness alone can help the LLM saturate the benchmark with a near perfect score then the combination of the two must still be effectively AGI in the sense of passing the most famous benchmark designed specifically to measure AGI progress, after multiple iterations of progressively making it harder. I think it is fair to say that this is probably effectively AGI if the benchmarks are remotely accurate - even with Fable, I've been at the point personally where I am reasonably confident that there's essentially nothing that I am better than Fable at despite generally being substantively above average on human benchmarks. If Astra's this much better than Fable, I'm ready to call AGI here. For the many people who resist the AGI label possibly ever being achieved, I'd be curious to hear takes on what would make you think Astra is yet to be AGI, and what would still need to be achieved for this to effectively be AGI from this point forward.

comments.author: abixb
comments.text: I want to take a step back: So, this is GPT-6 -- the natural number version release comparable to GPT-4 and GPT-5 from the past few years. The ARC-AGI-3 score is obviously impressive at 99.9% (we'll need to wait for more details on how they used the response API harness on GPT-6 Astra, wrt reasoning retention and compaction), but every other benchmarks seems to be a relatively modest improvement, comparable with any of the 'point' updates from AI labs. If this is truly AGI (subject to one's definition of AGI still), then this is a very boring release of an AGI model. No video announcement, no presser, just a blog post (with some Twitter promo vids)? As others mentioned, I'm starting to think OpenAI was under immense pressure to deliver an 'AGI' model for certain contractual reasons, but I never expected GPT-6 release to be this mundane and banal.

comments.author: manlymuppet
comments.text: I have nothing to say about the actual model, but unrelated--why do so many of these demos include people buying things autonomously? Even if I did trust an AI to get everything right, it's not like the AI can read my mind. If I was ordering food normally and without AI, I would want more control over the process--looking over the options, prices, thinking about what I really want. People don't know what they really want until they've thought about it a bit, so why do AI companies make it seem like a description is all that's required? All the context in the world cannot accurately predict how I'll react to things I haven't seen. The problem is people treating this like something that needs a solution. It doesn't. If you want to make my life easier with AI, just make it easier to do stuff. I don't want you to pick things that I actively enjoy picking myself. (Also not everyone has a cushy job in an AI lab that makes it so you won't miss $30 if the AI messes up haha.)

comments.author: astrobiased
comments.text: I can’t help but notice how much this echoes Francois Chollet’s On the Measure of Intelligence: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01547 Most of frontier-model progress still looks like skill acquisition optimization: broader benchmark coverage and performance, more domains absorbed into the training distribution, and increasingly strong performance within that surface area. It seems more about coverage-driven competence. Somewhat analogous to overfitting at scale. The harder question, in Chollet’s framing, is: how efficiently can a system learn to do something genuinely new? With our current AI architectures and training in place, I think we will only continue on skill acquisition optimization vs. truly novel intelligence.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、GPT‑6 AstraのARC‑AGI‑3スコアがほぼ満点に近いことから「実質的AGI」だと主張する意見と、スコアが特別なレスポンスAPIハーネスに依存しており他のベンチマークではわずかな改善しか見られないためAGIラベルは早計だとする意見の対立である。さらに、リリースがブログ投稿のみで大きな発表がないことへの失望感や、AIが勝手に商品を購入するデモに対する不快感（ユーザーの選択権を奪う危険性）が指摘された。注目コメントとして、フランソワ・チョレットの「On the Measure of Intelligence」を引用し、現在の進歩はスキル獲得の最適化にとどまり真の新規知能獲得には至っていないという洞察が挙げられた。また、ベンチマークのハーネス変更がスコアを水増ししている可能性を指摘し、AGI主張の根拠を疑う声もあった。これらが議論の中心となった。
stories.editor_note: GPT-6 Astra: 次世代言語モデルの噂が再燃し、日本企業もマルチモーダル対応の内製化を検討し始めた背景があります。国内スタートアップが基盤モデル依存を減らし、独自サービスの差別化を狙う動きと関連しています。

stories.title_en: Qwen 3.8 27B available on Cerebras at 1500 tokens/s
stories.title_ja: Qwen 3.8 27B は Cerebras で 1500 トークン/秒 で利用可能

comments.author: nostrebored
comments.text: 150k TPM limit on public endpoint means that it's likely unusable for many coding tasks. When we've tried Cerebras in the past, our problem has always been rates. We'd love to not deal with dedicated and to have access to a more flexible rate pool. Even trying it out, it seems like our account has gotten moved to some limbo where we can no longer add billing information. ``` Billing access restricted Self-serve billing is not available on Enterprise accounts. Please contact your team for further questions. ``` We have no team (they removed themself from our slack channel after we talked about rate limits). Perplexingly, none of this even shows up in the request, which gives: ``` {"message":"Model does not exist or you do not have access to it.","type":"not_found_error","param":"model","code":"model_not_found"} ``` When the error is really about billing. I always want to like Cerebras, but I get the vibe that as a tokens in tokens out consumer you are not valued at all.

comments.author: gpugreg
comments.text: I was wondering whether this was any good for programming, but it is too fast for its own good. There is a limit of 450,000 tokens per minute. I hit this limit in about 90 seconds and burned through $1.10 while doing so. This is because cached tokens count towards the token limit. For comparison, I ran the same task with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which finished in 172 seconds and cost $0.024 with a final context window size of 55217 tokens, while Qwen3.8-27B was not even close to being done with a 64178 context window. This is a very efficient way to burn your money, but I would not recommend it for programming. On the positive side, I got a $5 signup bonus, so it wasn't my own money.

comments.author: jasongill
comments.text: It would be great if they made their inference capacity for this model available via OpenRouter; the fastest provider on OpenRouter right now is at ~80tps https://openrouter.ai/qwen/qwen3.8-27b#providers They do appear to host other models on OpenRouter so maybe Qwen3.8 will be there soon: https://openrouter.ai/provider/cerebras

comments.author: pllbnk
comments.text: Just a couple days ago I learned about ninfer ( https://github.com/Neroued/ninfer ) and on RTX 5090 I can now get ~200 tok/s and over 400 tok/s on concurrent requests which is plenty fast for a local model of this strength.

comments.author: hexa00
comments.text: Just tried it on a medium size coding/debug problem on an existing codebase, observations: - Input doesn't look faster than other models, it spends a lot of time reading Read about 5M tokens - Output is awesome, super fast as you expect from the 1500t/sec I think that's correct - Tool call is failing more than say DS4, which leads to time wasted on retries (complex tools like browser control for example) - Shell commands are still somewhat of a bottleneck The net effect is that I spend about the same time waiting, and I still need to read that output so, at least for coding, it actually reconciles me with the 100-200t/sec you can get on DS4 or the like. Maybe that's a good sweet spot after all and faster t/sec is not where the bottleneck is. Also maybe my setup (OMP) doesn't do the cache correctly but that's a huge cost driver... so atm it's quite pricy

stories.summary_ja: 「Cerebras で提供される Qwen 3.8 27B は理論上 1500 tok/s と高速だが、公開エンドポイントの 150k TPM（≈450k トークン/分）制限やキャッシュトークンもカウントされるため、実際のコーディング作業ではすぐに上限に達し、数秒で数ドルのコストが発生するという指摘が多数。一方、出力速度は確かに速く、ツール呼び出しの失敗やシェルコマンドのボトルネックが目立ち、全体的な待ち時間は DS4 程度の 100‑200 tok/s と変わらないとの実測結果も。さらに、請求系の UI が企業アカウントでは制限され、サポートへの連絡が取りにくいなど、利用者側への配慮が欠けているという不満も。対照的に、OpenRouter への移管やローカルでの ninfer（RTX 5090 で ~200‑400 tok/s）など、柔軟なレートプールや自己ホストが望まれる声が上がっている。」
stories.editor_note: Qwen 3.8 27B は Cerebras で 1500 トークン/秒 で利用可能: Cerebras のウェーハスケールエンジンが低遅延推論を実現し、日本の金融機関がリアルタイムリスク解析への導入を検討している点が注目されます。従来のGPUクラスターよりコストパフォーマンスが向上すると見られます。

stories.title_en: .name Termination
stories.title_ja: .name 終了

comments.author: nneonneo
comments.text: It seems like the right thing they should do is discontinue new registrations but continue to honour existing ones (+ continuing to reserve any 2LD that has a 3LD registered on top). It’s a bit insane that they can decide to just terminate all existing 3LD registrations. One would hope that they’d at least continue to reserve the 2LDs for some period to avoid domain squatting, but this isn’t mentioned in the proposal and I doubt Verisign would graciously do so.

comments.author: jl6
comments.text: I can only assume somebody was asleep on the job when this scheme was approved, because the outcome is in direct contradiction to ICANN’s mission statement: > Its enduring mission is to ensure the stable, secure operation of the Internet's unique identifier systems. https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/about-icann Arbitrary termination of service is not stability. Enabling name hijacking is not security. The answer cannot be a rival name scheme based on decentralization or crypto or whatever. Those are never going to help normal non-wizard users. The answer has to be to make the regulators do their job.

comments.author: dvt
comments.text: I freaked out for a second because I've owned `dvt.name` for like 15 years. `.name` is not getting terminated, so it's important to be precise here. The third-level x.y.name (where you're the `x`) is getting terminated, and the respective `y.name` domains are going to be released. Still a crappy thing for people, but it does not affect owned second-level domains.

comments.author: nanolith
comments.text: This risk factor is similar to one I brought up during architectural review of an IoT company I helped to build. It's why the identity certificates our devices used were entirely disconnected from domain names, and why the discovery protocol I put together did not rely on registered domains, but could use these as an untrusted part of discovery. Domain names are leased. Things that are leased can disappear. The company leasing these assets could go bankrupt. They could weasel their way out of agreements as Verisign has done here. Any identity that is grounded in leased assets is built on shaky ground. It's also why I'm dubious of the way that e-mail addresses have become tied to online identity. I'm not saying that what Verisign has done is right, but this behavior is expected. Those of us who went through the (dot) bomb era remember just how shaky this infrastructure can be. I'm sorry that .name people are going through this. Even though it's a risk I expected, that doesn't make this okay.

comments.author: akersten
comments.text: It kind of seems like an insane TLD structure to begin with, right? I always thought .co.uk was bad (you're just pinning yourself to whoever owns the .co. part, but at least browsers have some suffix list where you can't, I don't know, hijack some login cookie for all of .co.). Joe Smith and John Smith can independently register joe.smith.name and john.smith.name, do browsers have a wildcard suffix list for the 2nd level of `.name` specifically, or can Joe set a cookie on all of .smith.name?

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Verisignが.name TLDの第三レベルドメイン（x.y.name）の登録を終了し、対応する第二レベルドメイン（y.name）を開放する方針についての批判と懸念。既存登録の継続を求める声と、レンタル性のドメインへの依存が危険という指摘。賛否は、新規登録停止は妥当だが既存権利の保護が必要という意見と、サービス終了は契約上許容されると見なす意見に分かれた。注目コメントでは、第三レベルのみの終了であり第二レベルは影響しないという事実の指摘、ICANNのミッションとの矛盾を指摘する声、IoTの事例からドメイン依存の脆さを警告した意見、そしてブラウザのサフィックスリストと.cookie hijackの可能性について疑問を呈したものが挙げられた。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、AIがエンジニアのスキルを維持・向上させるべきか、むしろAIに依存することで技術が劣化するリスクがあるかという点だ。特に、記事自体がAIによって生成されたことに対する皮肉や、「最適化されたシステムが無能なオペレーターを生むならそれは最適化ではない」という指摘が注目を集めた。これに対し、一部のコメントはAIが単なるツールであり、適切な教育や人間の監督システムを整えればスキルの喪失を防げると主張し、逆にAIが人間の注意力を低下させる「オペレーターのジレンマ」（原子力発電所のオペレーターや自動運転車の人間介入システムに例えられる）を懸念する声があった。賛否は、AIによるスキル低下の警戒感と、AIを活用した新たな学習・支援の可能性の間で分かれており、特に「人間が関与しないときに失われる状況認識」の重要性が共通の関心事となった。注目コメントでは、原子力プラントと自動運転車の事例を挙げて、AIがエラーを見えなくするだけで根本的な問題を解決していないことを指摘し、スキル維持のための設計原則の見直しを求める洞察が示された。
stories.editor_note: AI時代におけるエンジニアのスキルの保護: AIコード生成が進む中、日本のエンジニアはアルゴリズム思考とシステム設計能力を再評価すべきだと指摘されています。国内の技術教育機関では基礎理論の復習ワークショップが増えています。

stories.title_en: GLP-1s Are Being Linked to Fewer Serious Infections, Including TB
stories.title_ja: GLP-1s は重篤な感染症、結核を含めて少なくなることが関連付けられている

comments.author: master_crab
comments.text: Using a large database of (deidentified) medical records, the researchers compared the outcomes of people taking a GLP-1 for their type 2 diabetes to people taking other common diabetes drugs between 2017 and 2025. GLP-1 users were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with TB for up to a five-year span, they found. Both of these studies are observational and retrospective, meaning they can only show a correlation between GLP-1 use and reduced (or at least less severe) infections, not prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship. At the same time, these are the only latest pieces of evidence pointing to a genuine germ-busting benefit from GLP-1 drugs. I wonder if the likelihood that people taking a GLP-1 are probably better off financially, have a health care provider willing to spend on the drugs (and therefore probably a better medical system) or a combination of these and other traits are the real reason there are fewer infections.

comments.author: tarxvf
comments.text: How expensive are GLP-1s again?

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
GLP-1受容体作動薬が結核を含む重篤な感染症の発生率を低下させるという観察研究結果について、これが薬剤自身の免疫調整作用による直接的な効果なのか、それとも使用者の社会経済的背景や医療アクセスの質などの交絡因子によるものなのかが議論の中心だった。

・賛否両論  
賛成側は、GLP-1が炎症経路やマクロファージ機能に影響を与える preclinical データを挙げ、真の「菌撃退」効果の可能性に期待を示した。一方、懐疑派は研究が観察的・後向きであることを指摘し、使用者が一般に経済的に余裕があり、質の高い医療を受けやすいという選択バイアスが結果を説明できると主張した。また、薬剤の高コストが実際の使用者層を限定している点も懸念材料となった。

・注目コメント  
「GLP-1使用者はおそらく経済的に恵まれ、積極的に医療投資を行う医療制度に属しているため、感染率の低下は薬剤そのものではなく、こうした背景要因が本当の原因ではないか？」という指摘が特に洞察に富んでおり、交絡因子を考慮した解析の必要性を改めて浮き彫りにした。
stories.editor_note: GLP-1s は重篤な感染症、結核を含めて少なくなることが関連付けられている: GLP-1受容体作動薬が免疫調整に影響し、結核罹患率低下のエビデンスが出始めたことが注目されます。日本では糖尿病患者が多いため、併用による公衆衛生への波及効果が期待されています。

stories.title_en: Which tools do Claude, Codex and Cursor choose? We measured 17k runs to find out
stories.title_ja: Claude、Codex、Cursor が選ぶツールは？ 私たちは 17k 回の実行を測定してそれを突き止めました

comments.author: ex-aws-dude
comments.text: In the future: "I went ahead and built the database you requested using today's tool sponsor: Firebase"

comments.author: screm
comments.text: Hey! Disclaimer: I am a Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26) which sells growth services to dev tools. This study is part of our broader work on how to influence coding agents choices and get products picked. To understand how agents pick tools we measured close to 17k sessions on an environment where agents run exactly like in the real world, on various repositories, talking to different personas (vibe-coder, junior or senior engineers) in different sizes of companies. All the results are now public and we'd love to know what findings surprise you the most, here are a few we found interesting: - Claude Code rarely searches the web while Codex almost always does it and Cursor sits in the middle. - Coding agents disagree more frequently than they agree. - Some players (LangChain, Supabase, Netlify, Paypal, Adyen) are almost always mentioned in their categories but never chosen. - Modifying repository context can change the pick entirely. If you feel like digging, all the traces are there and we probably missed interesting learnings so let us know what you find!

comments.author: drivingmenuts
comments.text: I smell a money-making opportunity.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、Armatureの共同創業者が公開した約17,000回のAIコーディングエージェント（Claude Code、Codex、Cursor）の実行結果についてである。Claudeはウェブ検索をほとんどせず、Codecはほぼ毎回検索し、Cursorはその中間であり、エージェント同士の選択は同意よりも不一致が多いこと、LangChain、Supabase、Netlify、PayPal、Adyenなど特定のツールは頻繁に言及されるが実際には選ばれないこと、リポジトリのコンテキストを変えると選択が大きく変わることが指摘された。  

賛否については、あるコメント者がAIが好むツールが将来的に主流になり、選択が集中する可能性があると肯定的に捉えた一方、別のコメント者はこれを金儲けの機会と見なし、やや skeptical な姿勢を示した。  

注目すべきコメントとして、研究者自身が「エージェントがツールを選ぶメカニズムを影響させ、製品を選んでもらう方法」を探っている点が挙げられ、これがツールベンダーや開発者にとって戦略的示唆になるという洞察が得られた。
stories.editor_note: Claude、Codex、Cursor が選ぶツールは？ 私たちは 17k 回の実行を測定してそれを突き止めました: 大規模実験で、AIコードアシスタントが好むエディタやプラグインのパターンが明らかになり、日本の開発者も同様のツール選定に参考にできます。これにより、ローカル開発環境の標準化が進む可能性があります。

stories.title_en: Porting my 1993 Amiga game to Godot, with an LLM reading the 68000 assembly

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、LLM（Claudeなど）を用いて1990年代のアセンブリで書かれたAmigaゲームを読み込み、Godotなどの現代エンジンに移植できるかという実験的取り組み。参加者は、オリジナル開発者の苦労への敬意と、ドキュメントが乏しかった当時のデバッグ体験に共感しつつ、AIがバイナリからソース相当のコードを生成できる驚きを共有。賛否については、AIによる逆アセンブリが法的にグレーゾーンになる可能性や、生成コードの可読性・保守性に懸念を示す声と、忘れられたゲームを救済する手段として大きな可能性を見出す意見が分かれた。注目コメントでは、Amigaハードウェアリファレンスマニュアルを手にした懐かしさと、当時の開発物語を聞きたいという要望、さらにLLMが移植手順をエンジニアリングガイドとして出力できる仕組みの提案が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 私の 1993 年の Amiga ゲームを Godot に移植し、LLM が 68000 アセンブリを読み取る: レトロハードウェアのバイナリをLLMが解析し、現代のゲームエンジンへ自動変換する実験が行われました。日本のインディー開発者も、過去のアセットを活用したリメイクプロジェクトに活かせる手法として注目されています。

stories.title_en: K2 Horizon: A connected fleet of six open models
stories.title_ja: K2 Horizon：6 つのオープンモデルからなる接続されたフリート

comments.author: jjordan
comments.text: Fully open models really need to be a big part of the AI future. That includes all source code, open training data, how it's organized, fed to the model, processed, etc. Until that becomes a thing you're always going to be left wondering what exactly lies underneath the closed model you are using, leaving open the possibility for societal manipulation.

comments.author: a11r
comments.text: It is great to see another player introduce a fully open stack. Nvidia's Nemotron is the only other prominent one I know of. All that said, the headline claims do not match the self-reported performance. For example, the dense 32B model is significantly behind Qwen3.8 27B (chart towards the bottom of https://ifm.ai/blog/k2 ). Gemma4 31B is not in the comparison set. This is the most important sweet spot for self hosted open-weight models today and real competition here will be very welcome.

comments.author: piinbinary
comments.text: A bit off topic, but I think I'm starting to get model fatigue. These come out 10x faster than new Javascript frameworks were coming out 10 years ago (at least new models are far easier to adopt).

comments.author: cogman10
comments.text: My quick review of the 3.7B model (because I was interested) is that it's not to be trusted for coding. It failed my basic test I like to ask models and generated incorrect code. When prompted about the bug, it preceded to start hallucinating non-existent APIs. After doing that it got caught in a loop trying to desk check the solution that didn't work.

comments.author: cesarvarela
comments.text: I find it funny that while these releases are a technological miracle, the charts in the doc use tiny fonts and are hard to read. Goes with the idea that coding might be solved, but taste isn't.

stories.summary_ja: 「完全オープンなAIスタックが必要だ」という意見が中心で、ソースコード・学習データ・パイプライン全体を公開すべきだと指摘。K2 Horizonはそれを実現し、NvidiaのNemotronに続くもう一つの主要フルオープンモデルとして歓迎された。一方で、ベンチマークチャートが自己報告と食い違い、32B密モデルがQwen3‑8 27Bより劣るとの指摘や、Gemma4 31Bが比較に入っていないことから性能主張への疑問が出た。また、リリース頻度がJavaScriptフレームワークのラッシュに例えられ「モデル疲れ」を感じる声や、3.7Bモデルがコーディングテストで誤コードを出し、バグ指摘後に架空APIを hallucinate しループに陥った例もあり、実用性への懸念が示された。さらに、ドキュメントのフォントが小さくグラフが読みにくいという指摘もあり、技術進歩と可視性・使いやすさのギャップが話題になった。
stories.editor_note: K2 Horizon：6 つのオープンモデルからなる接続されたフリート: 複数のオープンLLMを連携させることでタスクごとに最適なモデルを動的に選択するフレームワークが登場し、日本の研究機関ではマルチモーダル推論基盤として評価されています。単一モデルへの依存リスクを分散できる点が魅力です。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、人工ビーバーダムが juvenile coho サーモンの生存率を8％から60％に向上させたことと、その結果水温が低下したメカニズム（地中への浸透と熱交換）である。また、ビーバーの再導入ではなく人工構造物を選んだ理由や、ダムが餌資源や食物連鎖に与える波及効果について疑問が呈され、ワシントン州での法規制が人工ダム設置を困難にしている現状も指摘された。賛否では、生態系回復とサーモン保護の効果を評価する声が多い一方で、単にビーバーを復帰させれば十分ではないか、あるいは予期しない生態系への影響を懐疑的に見る意見が見られた。特に注目されたコメントは、ワシントン州では水路へのいかなる変更も違法であり、農家が黙って水路を整備している現状を挙げ、法整備の必要性を訴えた点と、ビーバーダムによる水温低下の論文へのリンクを共有した科学的根拠を示した意見である。
stories.editor_note: 人工のビーバーダムにより、若齢のコホサーモンの生存率が 8% から 60% に上昇した: ビーバーダムの人工設置が魚類の幼魚保護に効果的であることが実証され、日本の河川環境保全プロジェクトでも同様のアプローチが検討されています。生態系復元と防災の両立が期待されます。

comments.author: no_multitudes
comments.text: I drew a woman born in 715 CE in the Yangtze Basin. It claims that 96% of women were married, the average age of marriage was 18, and 44% of women died before age 15. Clearly these facts can't all be true simultaneously. The firt citation for marriage data is listed as "Hajnal (RH31)", but links to a seemingly unrelated WorldCat search. The second citation is to "Kaplan (RH03)", which I was able to track down on sci-hub. It is a broad theory of human evolution that doesn't appear to mention the Yangtze Basin or China. Another citation is to "[RH109] Model-supplied gap-fill (Claude Fable 5 and Claude Opus 5, 2026-08-05). Bounds and items written to close gaps no dataset we hold covers. Not a published work: see each row's `basis` for its stated reason. (2026)" -- this is an interesting way to describe having an LLM hallucinate something for you. Please stop making vibe-coded websites -- it is not useful to provide incorrect facts. You are polluting the commons with garbage.

stories.summary_ja: 「Yangtze Basinで715年生まれの女性」をランダムに選出したプロジェクトについて、96％結婚、平均婚齢18歳、15歳以前死亡44％という統計が同時に成り立たない点が指摘された。さらに、引用先はHajnal論文へのリンクが関係なく、Kaplan論文は進化論全般で中国特有のデータを含まず、最後に「Model‑supplied gap‑fill（Claude Fable 5／Claude Opus 5, 2026）」と明記され、LLMが hallucinated データを補填していることが暴露された。これによりデータの信頼性が疑問視され、 vibe‑coded サイトとして批判された。別の意見では、ランダム抽出の確率分布が間違っており、現代に近い出生が極めて少ないことも指摘された。一方で、将来的に個人データが蓄積されれば本当の自叙伝が作れる可能性があるとし、AI生成ライフストーリーの面白さや、 Thousand Year Old Vampire などの物語系RPGへの応用を期待する声もあった。全体としては、面白い実験だがデータの正確性と出典の杜撰さが主な論争点となっている。

stories.title_en: Xanadu was waiting for agents
stories.title_ja: Xanadu はエージェントを待っていた

comments.author: ameliaquining
comments.text: This post buys into the common narrative about Xanadu, that it was a fundamentally good idea that failed due to some combination of poor execution, being too far ahead of its time, and the market not caring about quality (with this post in particular focusing mostly on the second thing). In my view, Gwern makes a compelling counterargument: Xanadu was a fundamentally bad idea. The parts of it that weren't incorporated into the World Wide Web either solved problems no one actually had, or couldn't have constituted a stable equilibrium between users and publishers (i.e., even if it'd been magically willed into existence, it'd have quickly fallen apart). https://gwern.net/xanadu

comments.author: ThinkBeat
comments.text: This sounds like one agent at each junction point, that may or may not be running the same model and architecture as the previous one, and they need to constantly crawl each other or just a protocol to call each other. But then you have a million of then constructing a docuverse web all having an agent who all need to know each other and its all connections and each a database repository. Well you only need links that exist, and those that are created. In a paragraph it may exist in one node that is referenced and that node may be a collection of other nodes, or each sentence or even each word points to other nodes, how much does each model know and what does it keep in its database. A point to the next node is not necessarily durable or versioned, and that goes for each node is connects to. A single paragraph could have thousands or more sources, references, and each source would need versioning and depending on version it may well point to different nodes in prior or future versions. A proper version of a paragraph would then need to know this, or expect that all nodes with an agent will be durable and rational and interoperable but if you build on that premise it will not work in the real world. All unless you keep the docuverse limited in scope to a few data stores and agents who comprehend that spatial universe, and it is a form of an intranet

comments.author: e12e
comments.text: Interesting. This and the other posts I've seen about Delta seems to exist in that liminal space, were it's difficult to tell if the author has had a brilliant insight, that they struggle to convey to anyone who's not yet had the same insight; or if they've simply gone slightly mad. It's a similar sense I get with reading Nelson (after being able to think about his ideas for a while, I'm quite certain it was mostly genius and only a little bit of lunacy). It remains to see how Delta will turn out. On a side-note; my initial reaction to the headline was; no. Xanadu wasn't missing agents. I do think I see where the author is going, though; and I think I agree that agents might be a new tool that might facilitate some hypertext ideas. Not Xanadu perhaps. But some other, more pragmatic and less magic place - but a place that is a little more magical than where we are now. And it intersects a bit with an experiment we started at work; migrating our modest web site from WordPress to a static site combining 11ty ( https://11ty.dev ) (we already lean heavily on typescript for our application development) and visual studio code with frontmatter cms ( https://frontmatter.codes ) - and AI/LLMs. AI helps with making a static page version of our site, and adopting to 11ty. The idea is that with trivial push-to-deploy setup, our business people, with the help of AI in vs code, will be able to work directly with 11ty and git to make changes, do reviews and publish changes. A hill that would probably have been too steep for them to climb just six months ago. So in reference to the theme of realizing a better hypertext system with the help of AI, we're sort of doing the same thing, it turns out: mix solid, boring tools (static site gen, typescript, editor, version control, CI, static hosting) and some AI - to hopefully allow more users leverage both tooling and AI in an empowering way. We've just stated the experiment - we may yet fly too close to the sun, and end up falling back to a traditional CMS.

comments.author: tolerance
comments.text: One of my favorite LLM-smells to train myself to sniff out is how well the author can tie two seemingly disparate ideas together into something compelling or novel. The more ambitious the synthesis and the less impressed I am the more likely I am to assume it was at least partially the work of an LLM. Previously, "Jimi Hendrix Was a Systems Engineer" < https://spectrum.ieee.org/jimi-hendrix-systems-engineer >

comments.text: Reading this makes me wish someone would really try to make Project Xanadu a reality. A network built on Content Addressable Storage and a Version Control System is some thing I'd really like to see invested in.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Xanaduが失敗した理由が「時代に先行しすぎた」か「根本的に悪いアイデアだった」かという点。一方の意見では、実行の不備や市場の質への無関心が原因だとするが、他方では、WWWに取り込まれなかった仕組みは実際には需要がなく、安定したユーザーと出版者の均衡を築けなかったと指摘。また、各接点にエージェントを置くことでバージョン管理や参照の永続性が課題になるため、スコープを限定したイントラネット的な運用が現実的という見解もある。さらに、エージェントやLLMを活用したハイパーテキストの実験例として、静的サイトジェネレータとAIを組み合わせた社内プロジェクトが挙げられ、非技術者でも更新できる環境を目指している。注目コメントとして、XanaduをContent Addressable Storageとバージョン管理システムで再構築すべきだとする提案や、LLM生成臭を嗅ぎ取る訓練法の言及が挙げられる。
stories.editor_note: Xanadu はエージェントを待っていた: 量子コンピューティングプラットフォーム Xanadu が、量子エージェントによる自動アルゴリズム探索の基盤を準備中であることが明らかになりました。日本の量子スタートアップも同様のハイブリッドアプローチを検討しており、競争が激化しています。

comments.author: rao-v
comments.text: It’s worth understanding that Shin Jinse has been significantly stronger than his nearest human opponents for a while now, more so than Magnus was even at his very peak. In go ELO like scoring he’s something like 120 points over the next strongest player. No other player has ever broken a 3800 rating let alone 3850. Ke Jie (the previous long time champion) peaked at 3755. Shin Jinseo’s strength graph is the most absurd straight line. https://www.goratings.org/en/ 2 stones is historically the gap between a 9P ranked and a 1P ranked professional player (very roughly the gap between super grandmasters and an almost grandmaster) That is to say it’s shocking that Katago (almost certainly significantly stronger than AlphaGo) is a mere 2 stones stronger than Shin Jinseo. I suspect it would be 3-4 stones vs any other human pro.

comments.author: thangalin
comments.text: In Go, there are exchanges of plays called "joseki". Professionals consider the outcome of joseki to be an equal result for both players. Most joseki are only a handful of moves, but some, such as the "flying knife" joseki have variations that continue for upwards of 50 moves. A traditional 19x19 go board has 361 intersections. Shin's genius was to play out a complex variation of the flying knife joseki that was, in essence, a one-way path to reach an equal board position that occupied about 1/4 of the board. Due to the 2-stone handicap, the position favoured black with the game ~25% complete. KataGo could not have played any other way, where a human may have tried to foil the plan by introducing further complications. What was truly incredible was how Shin held the advantage from that point on.

comments.author: PenanceAU
comments.text: The headline is a bit misleading, though perhaps not intentionally. Shin took a 2-stone handicap from KataGo which means that Shin is the weaker of the two. But to give that more context, Shin is also the strongest human player to have ever lived in raw strength terms by a good margin, and is known as replicating AI move-for-move more closely than anyone else. If they were to play even then there’s no chance any human could win (and pretty much all pros agree with that). Lee Sedol beating AlphaGo in game 4 of that series is largely considered the last time a human beat a modern AI in an even game, which is why it was so amazing. RE the game, Katago was set to use the strongest available model and ran on a 3x 3090 GPU system, which is a lot for KataGo. 20 seconds might sound like a handicap, but that’s over 100,000 play out variations which is essentially infinite for modern KataGo models (anything over 10,000 is overkill). Shin played well in all games, but his strategy was to avoid complexity. KataGo reads out complex fighting like an absolute monster, so Shin was trying to play very very solid and very very calm so as to not give KataGo an in. The 2-stone handicap could be thought of as roughly 10-15 points of ‘buffer’. That’s massive in professional games, and that’s what Shin used to win. He played so overly solid that it sometimes cost a point or two, but it removed an opening for Katago to fight. He did this at the key opening and middle-game sections and never burnt through the full buffer of handicap points in the last two games. That’s why those games look kinda ‘boring’, it’s because Shin wanted them to be that way. Also note that KataGo probably could have won if its ’variance’ was tuned higher (basically it taking risks). Standard KataGo won’t take risks, it just wins with brute force. For handicap games though you can tune its willingness to start fights higher to prevent people from just playing ultra solid (like Shin did). Shin did an absolutely amazing job and he deserves all the recognition. Katago routinely beats professionals giving them 3-4 stones of handicap, so the win by Shin highlights to me how strong he is, but also just how well he understands how the AI ‘thinks’.

comments.author: xhevahir
comments.text: > "This series taught me that rather than trying to imitate AI, it is far more important to build the board according to my own style." It's never made sense to me that so many go players study AI go play in the hope of emulating it in a human game. We're not machines. We can't do thousands of Monte Carlo tree searches per second.

comments.author: dlevine
comments.text: Apparently 2 stones is a huge advantage. An estimate is that the computer is roughly 4-600 ELO stronger on an even match. Also, the human played a strategy tailored to that huge initial advantage. He said that the AI did not handle this particularly well, and played high probability moves instead of trying to lure him into a mistake. Also, even though this was the best Go engine, it was not running on a supercomputer, and had a relatively limited amount of time per move. So, this was an important victory for a human, but not a sign that humans are now stronger than AIs at Go.

stories.summary_ja: 議論の焦点は、世界最強の棋士である申眞諝がカタゴに対して2石のハンデを取った試合で勝利したことの意味である。申は人間として過去最高の実力格差を持ち、ハンデは9段と1段程度の差に相当するため、カタゴがわずか2石しか上回っていない点に驚きが向けられた。申は飛ぶナイフの定石を複雑に展開し、盤面の約1/4を使って均衡点を作り出し、ハンデによるバッファーを活用して複雑な闘いを避け、カタゴの読み深さを封じた。賛否では、この勝利は人間の驚異的な適応力を示す一方で、カタゴがリスクを取る様にパラメータを変更すれば勝てた可能性があり、偶数局では依然AIが優勢だと指摘する意見もある。注目コメントとして、「自分のスタイルで盤を作ることがAI模倣より重要」という申の言葉や、ハンデを10～15点相当のバッファーと見なし、固守戦略が勝因だったという分析が挙げられた。

comments.author: kjshsh123
comments.text: >In contrast to a classic RNN, there's no unbounded hidden state accumulating across an entire trajectory I don' understand this line. In a classic RNN hidden state is bounded dimension. In fact it's transformers that technically have unbounded hidden state. You can't parallelize classic nonlinear RNNs for various reasons but in training both RNN and Transformer depend on the entire sequence history in a way that is unbounded. Of course in practice you just train on a max sequence length. RNN xhat[t+1]=f(x[t],h[t]) Transformer/self-attention xhat[t+1]=f(x[t],h[t],h[t-1],...,h[1])

comments.author: anon373839
comments.text: Sebastian Raschka posted about this architecture: > A lot of hype around OpenAI's Astra model here on my timeline today. Apparently, this goes back to a new article from The Information, which said Astra is a "recurrent depth or looped transformer". > It's always interesting to read about new or different approaches (including rumors about what the closed labs may be up to), but let's debunk this a bit. > About 2 months ago, I shared the architecture details of Nanbeige, for example, where "Nanbeige4.2-3B is pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens with a Looped Transformer that reuses the layer stack to increase capacity without adding parameters." > Yes, that's it. The looped transformer idea is just reusing layers in the transformer block. > In the case of Nanbeige, the main idea is to reuse the same 22-layer stack (=transformer block) twice instead of once. So, effectively it extends the 22-layer architecture to 44 layers, but without duplicating the weights. > In simple terms, this roughly doubles the size of the model (if we ignore the embedding and output layers for a second). But instead of requiring 2x the storage and RAM to host this model, it stays at the same size since we reuse the components. However, it's almost 2x as expensive in terms of compute, because we run the embedded text through almost 2x as many layers. > Why? In the Nanbeige 4.2 technical report, the researchers found that two passes gave the best trade-off and retained about 75% of the token efficiency of a standard architecture. (More passes gave barely any gains but made the training much slower and much more expensive.) > While, as far as I know, Nanbeige 4.2 is the first notable open-weight model that adopted this approach, the idea goes back to the NeurIPS paper "Mixture-of-recursions: Learning dynamic recursive depths for adaptive token-level computation". Actually, this paper proposes a mechanism that is a bit more sophisticated by adding a learned router that determines whether each token receives one, two, or more passes. So, easy tokens can exit early while harder tokens receive additional computation. > In sum, Astra may be a really good model, but this shouldn't be about this "looped transformer aspect," which is just a tiny architectural tweak. https://x.com/rasbt/status/2095141254958858496

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、OpenAIが噂されるAstraモデルの「ループド・トランスフォーマー（再帰的深度）」が実際に性能向上に寄与するかどうかである。一部はSebastian RaschkaのNanbeige例を挙げ、同じ層スタックを再利用するだけでパラメータ数は増えず、ストレージは変わらないが計算量はほぼ2倍になり、トークン効率は標準の約75%にとどまると指摘し、これが単なる architektonic tweakに過ぎないと見なす。これに対し、再帰によってトークンごとに計算深度を変えるMixture‑of‑recursionsのルーターアイデアや、人間の思考プロセスに近いと捉える意見があり、Chain‑of‑Thoughtが論理的経路を表さないという指摘とも関連づけられている。注目コメントでは、 classic RNNの隠れ状態は次元的に有界であり、Transformerが実際には未制限の履歴を参照するという指摘があり、再帰アーキテクチャの違いを明確にしている。

comments.author: boomlinde
comments.text: I've given up on Audacity because it hasn't kept up technically with how a typical home studio Linux system does audio, and looking at the change log it seems like they haven't addressed any of the problems I have with it in version 4. You'd think, well, it supports JACK, so you're gold on both JACK and Pipewire, but they only do this in an extremely annoying way. It doesn't create a persistent JACK client. Only when you start playback or recording does it temporarily create a JACK client which disappears when playback or recording stops taking any connections you've made to it with it. The temporary JACK client then must autoconnect to a sink or source, for whatever reason that is neither a limitation of PW nor JACK. So you'll undo this jank with an automatic connection manager, right? You'll configure it to immediately disconnect from whatever Audacity decided to connect to and automatically connect it to the source you want to record. Well, they've given the short-lived JACK client the brilliant and informative name "PortAudio", which is of course shared by other applications using portaudio. Even more brilliantly, the I/O ports are given new names on each new client! Some while ago I started Audacity up (having forgotten that it's broken) and got invited to a user survey. There was no concern at all in the survey about the thing that Audacity fundamentally does. Do I want it to be a DAW? Do I want to be able to buy plugins within it? Do I want AI features? Merely being asked these questions while their broken JACK implementation persists pissed me off. I want it to record and play back audio first of all. Audacity 4 looks like it's in the bizarre situation where it kind of looks like a well-designed DAW but behaves like it doesn't care about audio.

comments.text: Isn't CYP2D6 inhibition the surer and more convenient route? Adding a bulky isopropyl group might reduce affinity at sigma1 receptors. Think about it: Going from 3-methoxy to 3-hydroxy makes for a very different drug. Wouldn't you expect that going from 3-methoxy to 3-isopropoxy would also make for a very different drug -- and not just "the same thing but more resistant to first-pass oral metabolism"? Selective deuteration seems like another potential option with good prospects. Here it reduced CYP2D6 metabolism in a broadly similar case: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8724172/ Deuteration in a position like that is so simple that you can do it at home.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、エドガー・アラン・ポーの作品の本当の恐怖が「告白」にあるという記事の主張に対し、コメント欄ではポーの生涯における貧困や嫉妬、死の謎がその文学的才能をどのように色濃く反映しているかが焦点となった点です。また、当時の雑誌業界の経済状況と現在のデジタルメディアの対比から、当時の出版コストや読者層の違いが話題に上がりました。

賛否両論としては、ポーの天才は生活苦や人間関係のトラブルによってかえって際立つという見方と、彼の内面的告白こそが作品の核心であり、外部環境は二次的だという意見が分かれました。さらに、彼の死がモルフィン過剰摂取偽装だった可能性についても疑問が呈され、真相については議論が残りました。

注目コメントとして、研究ゲートへのリンクを共有し、ポーの告白と心理状態を新たな角度から分析した論文を紹介した投稿があり、これが議論を深めるきっかけとなりました。このリンク先の研究は、詩人の内面的葛藤と作品の恐怖感の間に直接的な因果関係があることを示唆しており、コメント欄で最も洞察に富んだ意見として挙げられました。
stories.editor_note: エドガー・アラン・ポーの物語の真の恐怖は、彼らの告白にある: ポー作品の心理的恐怖が告白という形式に起因することを指摘し、日本のホラークリエイターがナラティブ構造の見直しに活かしています。これにより、インタラクティブストーリーテリングにおける緊張感の設計手法が進化しています。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Pythonに導入が検討されている「lazy imports（遅延インポート）」の実用性と副作用についてです。コマンドラインツールや大規模ライブラリ（例：SciPy）の起動時間短縮・メモリ削減に期待が寄せられている一方、ライトインポートを無効にすると構文キーワード自体が使えなくなるため、循環インポートや型チェックなど、遅延が意味的に重要な場面では問題が生じるという指摘があります。賛否は、「遅延は意味的に重要でないべきで、 linting・テスト時には強制的に無効化できる仕組みが必要」という意見と、「try/exceptでモジュールの存在確認を行うパターンが遅延できず、存在チェック手段が欠けている」という懸念に分かれます。注目コメントとして、SciPyのメモリ肥大化を挙げて遅延インポートの必要性を強調しつつ、現在のtry/except形式では遅延が不可能なので、インポート時の存在確認APIを提供すべきだという洞察が示されました。
stories.editor_note: Python を遅延評価にする取り組み: Python に遅延シーケンスやジェネレータの仕組みを言語レベルで組み込む提案が進み、日本のデータサイエンティストはメモリ効率の高いパイプライン構築に期待しています。これにより、ビッグデータ処理における遅延評価の標準化が進む可能性があります。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
コメントでは、.arpa ドメインを取得して実際に使えるか、特にTLS証明書の発行が可能かが中心に議論された。多くのユーザーは .arpa が PTR レコード専用だと思い込んでいたが、実際は通常のゾーンファイルと同じように A/AAAA/TXT など任意のレコードを置けると指摘され、証明書発行の例（crt.sh の検索結果や実際に稼働しているサイト）が示された。一方、ほとんどの認証局（CA）が .arpa ドメインに対して証明書を発行しないという現実も共有され、Cloudflare の Advanced Certificates アドオンで返金トラブルに巻き込まれた体験談が挙げられた。さらに、Hurricane Electric（HE）が無料で割り振る IPv6 プレフィックスの有効期限や、ISP に rDNS 委譲を依頼すれば自分で PTR レコードを設定できるかという実務的な疑問も提起された。

**賛否両論**  
- **賛成側**：.arpa でも通常のドメインと同様にゾーンを自由に構築でき、TLS証明書は取得可能（crt.sh や実際のサイトが証拠）であり、HE の IPv6 プレフィックスは長期にわたって有効で、ISP に問い合わせれば rDNS 委譲も得やすいという意見。  
- **反対/注意側**：主要なCAは .arpa ドメインをサポートしておらず、証明書発行のために特別な手段（自己署名やプライベートCA）が必要になるため、実運用ではハードルが高い。また、HE のプレフィックスは使用していないと取り消される可能性があり、ISP からの委譲は交渉次第で不確実だという懸念も示された。

**注目コメント**  
特に洞察があったのは、「.arpa は単なるドメインであり、PTR だけに制限されるわけではない。A、AAAA、TXT など任意のレコードを置けるため、工夫次第で通常のサービスと同様に利用できる」という指摘。これにより、証明書取得の難易度だけでなく、.arpa ドメインの汎用性そのものが再評価されるきっかけとなった。また、HE の IPv6 プレフィックスの長期有効性について「実際にルーティングしていない限り失効しないが、将来のポリシー変更には注意が必要」との助言が挙げられ、実務的なリスク管理の視点が提供された。

comments.text: Author here. One thing that didn't make it into the post: there are no hand-drawn traces on this board. I find mouse-driven PCB layout maddening, so the whole card is a Python script driving KiCad's API—antenna coil, lettering, everything. Retuning the antenna meant changing one number and re-running the script, which as a hardware novice was the difference between finishing this and giving up. The chip is NXP's NTAG I2C Plus. I picked it for the energy-harvest pin (that's what lights the LED) and only realized later that it ships without NDEF formatting—which is why every consumer NFC app refused to touch it. Sending it raw write commands through Core NFC turned out to be much less scary than I expected: the part that matters is about 60 lines of Swift. I still can't get over JLCPCB assembling ten of these for about $75.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、NFCタップでバッテリーレスLEDを光らせる名刺サイズPCBの実装が興味深いが、同様のプロジェクトが増えてきて「リスクVのFPGA履歴書」のように使い古されているという指摘だった。賛否両論として、賛成側は作者がKiCadのAPIをPythonスクリプトで完全自動化し、アンテナチューニングを数値変更のみで行える点や、JLCPCBで10枚約75ドルと低コストで製造できたことを評価し、オープンソース精神やハードウェア初学者へのハードル下げを称賛した。一方、批判側は実用性が限られ、似たようなデモが続くと新鮮味に欠けるとの意見があり、NDEFフォーマットが欠如しているチップを選んだため一般のNFCアプリでは読み取れず、生の書き込みコードをSwiftで書く必要があった点が挙げられた。注目コメントは作者自身の説明で、マウス駆動のレイアウトを嫌いPythonで全設計をスクリプト化し、アンテナ調整も数字一つ変えるだけで済んだこと、そしてチップのエナジーハーベストピンを活用したLED点灯回路がSwift約60行で実装できたと語った点が特に洞察に富んでいた。
